name: Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance
summary: The Linux Foundation’s fund for open-source post-quantum cryptography: it hosts Open Quantum Safe, the PQ Code Package, CBOMkit and Longfellow ZK, paid for by members led by AWS, Cisco, Google and IBM.
intro: The Linux Foundation launched the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance (PQCA) on 6 February 2024 with eleven founding members: AWS, Cisco, Google, IBM, IntellectEU, Keyfactor, Kudelski IoT, NVIDIA, QuSecure, SandboxAQ and the University of Waterloo. Its stated aim is to be a central home for organisations and projects that need production-ready post-quantum libraries, to help them line up with the US NSA’s CNSA 2.0 timeline, and to make cryptographic algorithms easier to swap. It started with two projects, Open Quantum Safe, founded at Waterloo in 2014, and the new PQ Code Package. By October 2026 its members page listed four Premier members (AWS, Cisco, Google and IBM), twelve General members, among them Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Meta, SandboxAQ, Thales and Trail of Bits, and fourteen Associate members, including the University of Waterloo, MIT Connection Science and the US General Services Administration.

Like the GraphQL Foundation, the PQCA is a fund inside the Linux Foundation rather than a separate non-profit. A Governing Board of members sets the budget and priorities, and a Technical Advisory Council (TAC) coordinates the projects: one representative from each Premier member, up to seven, one academic or research representative, and representatives of eligible projects. The TAC elects a chair each year, who also sits on the board. Each project is a series of LF Projects with its own technical charter and steering committee, and contributing projects hand their name and accounts to the Linux Foundation; Open Quantum Safe’s steering committee, for example, includes people from Cisco, IBM Research, Microsoft Research and Waterloo.

The badge says a project is vendor-neutral and openly governed, not that it is ready to protect production data. The alliance deliberately hosts both research and production code: Open Quantum Safe’s liboqs carries dozens of candidate algorithms and warns against production use, while the PQ Code Package writes formally verified implementations of the NIST standards that AWS-LC and other libraries ship. The TAC adopted a lifecycle with stages for each track in August 2024, but as of October 2026 neither the alliance’s project page nor the projects’ own pages show which stage a project is in, so read each project’s README for its status.

sections.title: Projects
sections.intro: The four projects listed on pqca.org in October 2026. Only the first two produce cryptographic primitives.

rows.label: Open Quantum Safe
values: liboqs, a C library of post-quantum KEMs and signatures for prototyping and research, plus oqs-provider for OpenSSL 3, demos and language wrappers
Founded at the University of Waterloo in 2014 by Michele Mosca and Douglas Stebila; founding PQCA project in February 2024

rows.label: PQ Code Package
values: High-assurance, formally verified implementations of standard algorithms: mlkem-native, mldsa-native and slhdsa-c, plus Rust and Jasmin work
Created for the PQCA’s launch in February 2024, starting with ML-KEM

rows.label: CBOMkit
values: Tools to build and analyse cryptographic bills of materials (CBOMs), such as a SonarQube plugin that finds cryptography in source code (Go support was added in 2026), to inventory what needs migrating
Proposed by IBM maintainers in October 2025, Apache 2.0, onboarding completed on 4 December 2025; it asked to start in the Incubation stage

rows.label: Longfellow ZK
values: A zero-knowledge proof library for existing identity formats (ISO mdoc, JWT and W3C Verifiable Credentials), so a wallet can prove a fact such as age without revealing the credential
Open-sourced by Google in 2025 and donated to the PQCA on 2 September 2026

sections.title: The lifecycle on paper
sections.intro: The TAC approved a project lifecycle policy on 28 August 2024. Projects join one of two tracks, can switch with TAC approval, and every move between stages needs a two-thirds TAC vote.

items.name: Experimentation
items.text: Research code that is, or could become, important to post-quantum cryptography, from a fresh paper’s implementation to a long-lived tool with few maintainers. No requirements on community size; minimal foundation support.

items.name: Labs
items.text: Long-term research code with a large maintainer community and academic impact: at least five governing members with no more than a third from one employer, documented governance, a stable API and a list of research users. It gets a binding vote on the TAC.

items.name: Incubation
items.text: An early or small production project. Users are told to evaluate it carefully, since the stage sets no requirements on community, governance or production readiness.

items.name: Growth
items.text: A project with a growth plan, at least two independent production users, a steady flow of contributions and a stable API, expected to move on within two years.

items.name: Impact
items.text: Mature, widely used in enterprise production, with diverse maintainers, published adopters, release and long-term support plans, and a documented security policy, threat model and audit history. It gets a binding vote on the TAC.

items.name: Emeritus
items.text: Projects at or near end of life: the foundation keeps the name and domains, but the project is not actively developed and may only get security fixes.

sections.title: What the TAC works on
body: The TAC meets every two weeks in public and keeps its minutes on GitHub. Its 2026 chair is Aditya Koranga, and in October 2026 its roster of eight included representatives from Amazon, Cisco, Google, IBM, NVIDIA and zeroRISC. Besides admitting projects it runs working groups, first proposed in 2024 for algorithms, tooling, documentation and security, a blog with its own review process, and LFX mentorships, such as one in 2026 to add languages to CBOMkit.

In April 2026 the TAC voted to start a readiness tracking working group, proposed by Google, to build a vendor-neutral, crowdsourced record of which versions of cryptographic libraries and common open-source projects support post-quantum algorithms, so organisations know what they need to upgrade to.

story: Open Quantum Safe had been the main open-source test bench for post-quantum algorithms since 2014, with contributors from Cisco, IBM, Microsoft Research and others, while NIST ran its competition. With the first NIST standards expected in 2024, companies that would have to ship them wanted a neutral place to build shared, high-quality implementations. On 6 February 2024 the Linux Foundation announced the PQCA, with Open Quantum Safe finding what the announcement called a permanent home, and the PQ Code Package started to write production-grade code for the coming standards, beginning with ML-KEM.

The first year went on structure. The TAC formed in spring 2024, took proposals for working groups, and on 28 August 2024 approved the project lifecycle with its separate research and production tracks. The PQ Code Package released the first alpha of mlkem-native in December 2024 and v1.0.0 in June 2025; by then liboqs and AWS’s AWS-LC had both adopted it.

From late 2025 the alliance grew beyond algorithm code. IBM’s CBOMkit, tools for inventorying cryptography, became a project in late 2025, the TAC set up a readiness tracking working group in April 2026, and on 2 September 2026 Google donated its Longfellow zero-knowledge proof library for digital identity, saying it wanted vendor-neutral stewardship so others could trust, audit and adopt it.

choices.choice: A fund inside the Linux Foundation
choices.why: Using the LF’s directed-fund model gave members a governing board, legal home and staff from day one, while each project keeps its own charter and steering committee.
Prototyping libraries like liboqs and verified production code like mlkem-native have different goals, so the lifecycle judges each against the right bar instead of one maturity ladder.
Algorithm selection stays with NIST and other standards bodies; the alliance’s mission is software that helps adopters meet timelines such as CNSA 2.0.
Subtle bugs and timing leaks are the main risk in new cryptographic code, so the PQ Code Package proves its C and assembly correct rather than relying on testing alone.
